paper: Wetter et al. (2014), Modelica Buildings library, J. Building Performance Simulation 7(4):253-270
note: These are genuinely OPEN questions raised by (but not answered in) the Wetter 2014 paper and its subsequent evolution. They are grounded in the paper's own scope (Modelica-based whole-building simulation, TMY3 forcing, acausal fluid networks, validated Examples suite) and reflect gaps that the replication run also could not close.

questions.q: Under what conditions can the Modelica Buildings library be co-simulated with a full CFD engine (e.g. OpenFOAM or the FFD code Wetter et al. later described) to resolve detailed indoor airflow, and at what coupling frequency does the coupled system remain both stable and predictively better than the well-mixed zone assumption baked into Buildings.Examples.SimpleHouse and the other example models?
questions.basis: The paper describes the Buildings library as a lumped-parameter / well-mixed-zone simulator (e.g. the SimpleHouse zone the replication ran has a single zon.T state). The Airflow subpackage exists but only handles bulk inter-zone flow; there is no in-paper coverage of a CFD coupling. Independent airflow validation is left to external tools.
next_steps: Build a minimal test case coupling one Buildings zone model to a small CFD grid via FMI or via the Buildings.Utilities.IO.Python interface.

Sweep coupling step sizes (1 s, 10 s, 60 s, 300 s) under a step change in HVAC supply temperature and measure divergence between coupled-CFD zone-air temperature and the well-mixed Modelica prediction.
Identify the coupling frequency at which the added CFD cost is repaid by predictive gain, using a metric like RMS surface-temperature error against a reference finely-resolved CFD-only run.

questions.q: How should a Buildings-library model be calibrated when the real building instrumentation is sparse (e.g. only a single indoor air temperature sensor and a whole-building electricity meter, as is typical for existing residential and small commercial stock) --- and how much of the paper's implicit whole-building fidelity survives after such calibration?
questions.basis: The replication used the paper's ready-made SimpleHouse example with designer-chosen parameters (QHea_flow_nominal=700 W, setpoint 20 C). The paper's Examples suite exists as forward-simulation demos; it does not describe an inverse workflow for identifying envelope, infiltration, and HVAC parameters from field data. Real deployments almost never have full sub-metering.
next_steps: Instrument a real (or high-fidelity synthetic) building with only 1-2 sensors + a utility meter; use the Buildings library forward model as the calibration target.
Compare Bayesian (e.g. MCMC) vs. gradient-based (via Modelica's own AD, or via surrogate) parameter identification on the same instrumentation-poor case.
Quantify posterior parameter uncertainty and forward-predictive uncertainty on out-of-sample months; report which envelope parameters are identifiable from sparse data and which are not.

questions.q: What model-reduction techniques (e.g. modal truncation of the linearised envelope, block-structured RC-network extraction, POD of the fluid-network Jacobian) allow the Buildings library to scale from single-building examples like SimpleHouse to a city-district or urban-block simulation of 10^3-10^5 zones, while preserving the paper's validated coupling of thermal and hydronic dynamics?
questions.basis: The replication ran a 1-zone SimpleHouse example for a year in 1.48 s wall-clock; the paper's contribution class targets whole-building HVAC + envelope simulation. Neither the paper nor the current v14 mainline documents a scale-out path to district or city scale, yet urban-energy-model demand is exactly where whole-building physics is now being asked to live.
next_steps: Baseline: linearly extrapolate SimpleHouse wall time to N buildings and identify where naive parallel scaling breaks (compile-time, solver, or I/O bound).
Extract equivalent 3-6 state RC networks per zone from the linearised Buildings models and benchmark full-Modelica vs. RC-surrogate district simulation on a shared TMY3 year.
Investigate ScalableBenchmarks (already in Buildings.Examples) as an existing test bed: measure real (not extrapolated) scaling to 10^2-10^3 zones and identify the dominant cost.

questions.q: For a hybrid workflow that uses fast reduced-order RC models for design exploration and full Modelica Buildings models for verification, what is the fidelity-vs-speed Pareto frontier, and where do the two families disagree qualitatively (not just quantitatively) on outputs like peak heating power, hours of thermal discomfort, and annual energy?
questions.basis: The replication observed SimpleHouse peak radiator power == 700 W (== nominal capacity) and annual heating ~1056 kWh --- exactly the kind of design metrics that industry increasingly computes via RC surrogates. The paper motivates full Modelica models on physical-fidelity grounds but does not benchmark them against RC-network alternatives on identical loads.
next_steps: Choose a matched pair: SimpleHouse (Modelica) and a 5R2C RC model with matched U-values, capacitances, setpoints, and TMY3 forcing.
Run both for a full year; compare not only annual energy but also the tails (worst 1% of hours) where RC surrogates typically fail.
Vary occupant / HVAC step-change intensity and identify the regime where the RC surrogate stops being fit-for-purpose; report as an operating-envelope condition rather than a scalar error.

questions.q: How should stochastic occupant behaviour (arrivals, departures, thermostat overrides, window opening, plug-load surges) be incorporated into Buildings-library simulations so that the plausible-trajectory claim demonstrated by SimpleHouse (zone.T in 20.0-24.5 C, radiator peak == 700 W) generalises to the far wider trajectory envelope that real occupants produce, without inflating simulation cost prohibitively?
questions.basis: SimpleHouse in the replication has no occupants, no plug loads, no window-opening model; the deterministic zone.T range of 20.0-24.5 C observed over a Chicago year is a lower bound on the realistic trajectory envelope. The paper acknowledges HVAC/controls modelling but treats occupant behaviour as exogenous / user-supplied. Real building energy is dominated by occupant variability.
next_steps: Wrap SimpleHouse with a stochastic occupancy generator (e.g. Markov-chain arrival/departure + stochastic setpoint overrides) and run 100-1000 Monte Carlo years.
Compare the ensemble spread of annual heating (currently the single value 1056 kWh) with the ASHRAE-style deterministic value; quantify occupancy-induced variance.

Evaluate whether Modelica's overhead (~1.5 s / simulated year for SimpleHouse) is compatible with Monte Carlo occupancy sweeps at portfolio scale, or whether a surrogate is required for the outer loop only.
